prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: Topological insulators identify a simple, general mechanism: band topology, captured by a Z2 invariant, forces robust boundary states that survive disorder. That is the kind of universal organising principle I look for. The idea was stated cleanly by Kane and Mele, tested decisively in HgTe quantum wells by Molenkamp's group, and then carried well beyond one material, into 3D insulators, photonic and mechanical analogues and cold-atom realisations. Seven members place it in their top four, and four of them in their top three. Nobody argues it is premature. Nearly twenty years of independent confirmation, with a stable interpretation, make this one of the best-understood discoveries on the shortlist. The 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and topological phases in the Chern/quantum Hall setting, and did not cover the Z2 classification, the quantum spin Hall state or time-reversal-protected edge and surface states, so I see no real overlap.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. A three-name limit excludes Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal is what directed the Molenkamp experiment, and also Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy and the ARPES groups (Hasan, Cava) who established the 3D case. Several colleagues, including Eriksson and Olsson, flag this too. If the committee judges that the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulators are separate compound discoveries, no three-person set fits both fairly. I am also working from memory on the priority chronology. And my own preference is partly temperamental: I favour clean theory with a mechanism, which may lead me to undervalue the instrument-driven and measurement-driven candidates.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B022 first and B039 second. She values the magic-wavelength idea as simple and original, and sees optical lattice clocks as stable, reproduced and mature, while noting that B039 is a genuinely new organising principle whose credit allocation is contested.
responses.response: I agree that B022 is mature, and its two-name attribution is far cleaner than B039's. That is a real advantage and I put it first among my alternatives. I still place B039 above it. A clean attribution does not outweigh the difference in scope. The clock is a refinement of precision built on the frequency-comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) lineage, while topological band theory is a new organising principle, as you say yourself. A contestable attribution can be managed by a carefully worded citation, whereas for a clock prize the boundary against the earlier prizes is a question the citation cannot remove.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B022 first as the strongest case on the list: a measurement technique that moves the limit of what can be observed, with independent confirmation across labs and a redefinition of the second in prospect.
responses.response: I accept that B022 delivers tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy, and I would not oppose it. But the redefinition of the second has not happened, and I would be wary of letting an anticipated metrological decision drive the prize. Impact on measurement is also not the same as a discovery about nature. Topological insulators changed what condensed matter physicists think a phase can be, which goes well beyond measurement. Where we may differ is on weighting: if the committee puts measurement precision above conceptual novelty, B022 wins, and I would not call that unreasonable.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B039 first and B035 third. He stresses the theory-experiment loop in topological insulators and the stable interpretation, but flags that the credit omits Bernevig, Zhang, Hasan, Moore and Balents, and says the trio is defensible but not uncontested.
responses.response: I agree on the strength and on the attribution problem. I would go further and say it should be settled in the citation wording instead of being left open. A citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation in HgTe makes Kane, Mele and Molenkamp coherent, and the 3D case then becomes an acknowledged adjacent achievement rather than an omission. I disagree with your ranking of B035 relative to the other candidates, though. The superconducting pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is unresolved, which I treat as a maturity concern that B039 does not share, so I would let B035 wait.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the GRB afterglow candidate B049 first as an instrument-enabled observational discovery, and places B039 fourth, noting that he defers to condensed-matter colleagues and that the 2016 prize touched topological phases.
responses.response: I take the B049 case seriously: it is a clean discovery of a natural phenomenon with decades of confirmation. But as you note yourself, the supplied credit leaves out optical-counterpart teams and theorists, and I cannot assess the BeppoSAX versus optical priority chronology independently. On the 2016 overlap, I disagree. The Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz prize concerned topological defects, phase transitions and quantized Hall conductance in a Chern-number setting. Time-reversal-symmetric Z2 physics is a different structure. I would not object to B049 as a second part of a two-part prize if the committee wants an astrophysics component, but I am not proposing it.

uncertainties: Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the 3D topological insulators should be treated as one achievement or two, and how the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission is handled.
Whether the committee puts conceptual novelty above metrological impact, which decides between B039 and B022.
I rely on memory for priority details and have not verified them independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. None of the credited candidates for B039, B022 or B025 is a documented collaborator or institutional colleague. I note only that GU and Chalmers physics are closely linked and that colleagues Johansson and Olsson are Gothenburg-based; no specific collaboration with any shortlisted candidate was found.
